groups.text: A rate cache holds two exchange rates.
Every few seconds, a refresher thread updates them, one put at a time.
Readers price payments with both.
The refresher writes the new EUR rate.
Before it writes GBP, a reader reads both.
What pair does it get?
The new EUR rate with the old GBP rate: a version that never existed.
Every put and get was thread-safe.
The map was shared, and it was changing.
A race needs both at once: state that more than one thread can reach, and a thread that changes it.
Take either one away, and there is nothing to lock.
First, take away the changes.
Each version of the map is built once, and never touched again.
The refresher builds the next version off to the side, where no reader can see it.
Then one volatile write points the field at it.
A reader that copied the field into a local before the swap keeps reading the old version.
Every reader sees one whole version, and nobody takes a lock.
Second, take away the sharing.
A local variable lives on one thread's stack, and no other thread can reach it.
A Kafka consumer can keep its partition's totals in a plain HashMap, because only its own thread touches them.
When work moves to another thread, ownership moves with it.
Put the batch in a queue, and never touch it again.
ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy.
But a pool thread keeps its copy for as long as it lives.
Request one sets the tenant to alice.
Request two lands on the same thread, and sets nothing.
Who does it run as?
alice. One merchant's context leaks into the next request.
So every set needs a remove in finally, and the thread goes back clean.
In code, the snapshot is a volatile field and an immutable copy.
Build it completely, then publish it in one write.
Readers take no lock.
So before you add a lock, ask which one you can take away: the sharing, or the changes.
Quick check. A producer puts a batch in the queue, then clears it to reuse for the next batch.
Which corner is that batch in now?
